newsitem.title: INDIA: British condom firm sees big business in India.
newsitem.headline: British condom firm sees big business in India.

text.p: India, the world's second most populous nation, is set for a sharp rise in condom use over the next decade from around one per person annually, a senior official at a British condom firm said on Thursday.

"We are very optimistic about the growth of market in view of the government's emphasis on use of condoms, particularly for prevention of AIDS and in view of the growing social awareness," said Clive Kitchener of London International Group Plc.
"In regard to India, it (consumption) is one use per capita in terms of practice. The opportunity, I think, is for double digit growth in the next 10 years," he told Reuters.
Kitchener is director of strategy at LIG, whose Durex brand controls 22 percent of the world's branded condom market.

According to India's National AIDS Control Organisation, nearly 53,000 people in the country of 930 million people are infected with the human immunodeficiency virus that causes Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome.
Kitchener was in India to launch two premium quality condoms made by a joint venture, TTK-LIG Ltd, in which LIG holds a 44 percent stake.
India's current annual consumption of condoms is placed between 1.1 billion and 1.4 billion. The figure was expected to reach up to 2.1 billion by 2000, a TTK group official said.
Kitchener said his group was banking on freer world trade to expand the market for condoms following liberalised rules formulated by the World Trade Organisation.
"It will be good for us for the custom duty will be much less and procurement of latex will be easier," Kitchener said.
LIG has eight manufacturing units spread over the United States, Europe and Asia.
"We are trading in 140 countries but getting special latex from Malaysia has been a problem sometimes because of high customs duty and once we had to buy locally," he said.
Kitchener said he expected the branded condom market in developed countries to grow by two to three per cent per year and by a higher rate in developing countries.
"The growth in the developing countries will be much more but it is difficult to quantify," Kitchener said.
